Topic 4 -Major Taxes -Land Taxes Slides -Slides 11 -12.   Property and Real Estate Major Taxes - Land Taxes Transfer of Land Act 1958 and the Torrens System of land registration. The Transfer of Land Act 1958 is the main statute that relates to the transfer of land in the Northern Territory. The Act adopted the South Australian Torrens System of land registration as it then existed, with some modifications. The Torrens System is a system of land registration which provides for the registration of title to land. The system was enacted in 1872 in South Australia and has been adopted in one form or another in all other States and the Australian Capital Territory. The key feature of the Torrens System is that it establishes a state guaranteed system of land registration. In other words, once land is registered, the State guarantees the title. Once a person is registered as the owner of land, they have the same rights as if they had held the fee simple title. The only way in which an owner of land can be ousted is through the process of compulsory acquisition. A fringe benefit is taxable if it is given to a person who holds a 'position of authority' in a company. This would generally include directors, CEO and other high level executives. Their entitlement to fringe benefits is likely to fall within the 'benefits provided to supervisory employees' category. A benefit is not a fringe benefit if it is provided by an employer to an employee during a 'deemed year of tax' (s 136(1) FBTAA). Similarly, an employer does not provide a fringe benefit when they provide an employee with a 'fringe benefit' as defined in s 136 (1). In these cases, the benefit is not 'provided by an employer to an employee' as required by the definition of a fringe benefit. In addition, certain benefits are specifically excluded from being fringe benefits. For example, benefits provided to assist an employee to purchase a car for use in employment are not fringe benefits (s 7(1)). Likewise, where an employer provides an employee with a 'fringe benefit' as defined in s 136(1), the benefit is not a fringe benefit if it is one of a number of benefits enumerated in s 23L ITAA36. These exemptions are discussed in more detail in the chapter 'Fringe Benefits Tax' in Foundations of Taxation Law (Barkoczy, 2017, ch 20, pp 456-457).
